transcript.text: my belling cooker keeps burnin stuff 1 day then next day its undercookd on same temp. been like it a cuple months. thermastat??

It could be, but I would not condemn the thermostat yet. If the whole oven is alternately far too hot and too cool at the same setting, a temperature-control fault is plausible: a dial-controlled oven uses a thermostat, while a digital-temperature oven normally uses a sensor and control. If it is mainly one side of the food, or the top/bottom, that is wrong, the more likely causes are poor fan circulation, a door seal not closing properly, or an element not heating in the selected mode. 1. Check the oven function each time: make sure it is not on grill or rapid/booster heat, and use the same shelf position. Fan-oven recipes normally need about 10–20°C less than conventional-oven recipes.
2. With the cooker switched off and cool, check the door closes evenly and the seal is not split, flattened or coming away. A gap can make temperatures unstable.
3. If it is a fan oven, listen during use for the fan running normally. A weak, noisy or non-running fan can cause unreliable cooking results. When it goes wrong, is the whole oven too hot/too cool, or is food mainly burning or undercooking on one side? That is the quickest way to separate thermostat/sensor trouble from a fan or heat-distribution fault.
its the whole oven i think, not just 1 side. the fan is going i can hear it. door seal is a bit flattened at the top corner but door shuts ok. its a main fan oven, top oven and grill are fine

With the whole main oven varying, while the fan runs and the other oven/grill are fine, the main suspect is the main-oven temperature control: usually the thermostat on a dial-controlled cooker, or the temperature sensor/control on a digital one. A weak or intermittent fan-oven element/connection is the next possibility. The slightly flattened seal may lose some heat, but is less likely to cause such large day-to-day swings on its own. 1. Put a separate oven thermometer on the centre shelf, set the main fan oven to 180°C, and leave it long enough to settle. Check the thermometer rather than judging by the thermostat light, which normally cycles on and off. • If it repeatedly sits far above or below 180°C, or swings very widely, that strongly supports a thermostat/sensor-control fault. • If the actual temperature is broadly stable but cooking is weak/slow, the fan-oven element or its connections move up the list. 2. When the oven is fully cold, switched off and isolated, visually inspect the circular element around the fan for a split, blister, hole or burnt-looking area. Do not remove panels or touch wiring. Visible damage would make the fan-oven element the likely fault. If the thermometer shows erratic temperature but the element looks intact, this is best booked as an engineer job: confirming the thermostat/sensor and checking the element connections involves internal electrical testing. The door seal is worth replacing if it becomes split, loose, or leaves a clear gap, but it is not my leading cause here.
dont have a thermometer sorry. the neon goes off after 10 mins some days but other days it seems to stay on for ages. the knob is a bit wobbly too. should i get an engineer?

Yes — I would get an engineer for this rather than carry on using the main oven for cooking that needs reliable temperatures. The changing behaviour of the heating neon supports a fault in the main oven’s heat-control circuit: most likely the thermostat if this is a dial-controlled oven, or its control/sensor arrangement if it has electronic temperature control. The loose temperature knob also needs checking; it could simply be a loose knob, but if the spindle/control behind it is loose or worn it can make the selected temperature unreliable. An intermittent fan-oven element connection or element is the next possibility. The neon going on and off by itself is normally expected once an oven reaches temperature. What is not normal is it behaving very differently from one day to the next and producing burnt food on one occasion and undercooked food on another at the same setting. Ask the engineer to check the main-oven thermostat/control, the temperature knob and spindle, and the fan-oven element and its connections. They will need to isolate the cooker and carry out internal electrical tests, so this is not a sensible DIY parts purchase from the symptoms alone. The slightly flattened door seal is worth noting, but it is unlikely to be the main cause of such large temperature swings.
